extracted.intended_audience: novelists, fiction writers, and students/critics of fiction
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on selecting and applying narrative methods (dramatic vs pictorial/omniscient), assigning point of view, and handling scene, background, and narrator so a novel best expresses its subject-matter. Emphasizes when to show by action and when to tell by summary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of a narrator (only when he adds value)
rubrics_metrics.description: The narrator should be used when his presence 'is made a value in itself, contributing definitely to the effect of the subject'; otherwise he is better dispensed with and a direct view of the matter is preferable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the subject only asks to be reflected and pictured, the spokesman (narrator) may be the best method because of economy and force. Anti-pattern: a narrator who exists merely for the convenience of the author and 'pours out his information' unnecessarily, embarrassing a vivid dramatic scene by forced narration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignment of point of view (whose consciousness tells the tale)
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide whether the progress of the tale lies in the consciousness of characters (their minds acting the story) or in the vantage of an external chronicler/narrator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: In some novels each character 'takes up the story' and 'they act it' rather than narrate (e.g., Wings of the Dove), whereas large chronicles require a chronicler's angle. Choose whichever point of view the subject demands.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose dramatic vs pictorial (summary) method according to subject
rubrics_metrics.description: A story may be treated as drama (presented in scenes, immediate action) or as a pictorial/summary subject (generalized account by a narrator); the nature and scale of the subject determines the proper method.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Large, expansive subjects (crowds, long time-span) are 'pictorial' and usually need a narrator/chronicler (Thackeray). Compact, action-limited situations can be presented scenically as drama (The Awkward Age).

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatizing interior life via outward signs
rubrics_metrics.description: An undramatic subject (concerned with impact of experience on a mind) can be made dramatic by using tell-tale gestures, speaking looks, and other objective signs so thought is expressed through action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make use of looks and gestures: 'express the story through them, leave them to enact it—and you have a story which in its manner is effectually drama.' This is useful when the inner life can be externalized convincingly (example: Strether).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency of method
rubrics_metrics.description: A novelist should consider maintaining a consistent method—either dramatic throughout or pictorial throughout—because mixed methods risk incoherence unless justified by the subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Awkward Age is cited as an example of strict, homogeneous dramatic method and its aesthetic value; but the text also notes strict consistency is difficult and rare. Mixing may be practical but should be deliberate, not accidental.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy: narrator as efficient summarizer
rubrics_metrics.description: Where appropriate, the narrator embodies the principle of economy—summarizing, picturing, and economizing on depiction to make the most of a pictorial subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the subject asks only to be reflected or pictured, the narrator can 'make the most of it.' Conversely, unnecessary narration wastes the immediacy drama can provide.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scale/amount of subject limits dramatic method
rubrics_metrics.description: If a subject extends beyond a certain amount (in time, space, complexity) it exceeds the capacity of pure dramatic method and requires summary or authorial survey.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A large, loose, manifold subject 'on the whole must be presented as a conspectus' with angle of vision assigned to a narrator; otherwise many scenes would have to be omitted or compressed awkwardly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelists' advantage over playwrights: controlling manner
rubrics_metrics.description: The novelist can not only write words but also create the manner in which they are spoken, ensuring an 'ideal pitch' of expression that a playwright cannot guarantee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When choosing a scenic/dramatic form, remember the novelist's capacity to fix the manner (stage-direction-like detail) provides tighter control of interpretation than a playtext left to actors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations of pure drama in expressing background and associations
rubrics_metrics.description: Purely dramatic (play-form) fiction is hampered in its power to express outlying associations, background, and atmospheric breadth; drama is vivid but narrow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the effect of the action depends on time, place, or social background, the novelist may need broader survey or pictorial summary to make the setting's colour and associations fully felt. Otherwise the background 'will fail to make its full impression.'

rubrics_metrics.name: When background/setting is essential prefer pictorial support
rubrics_metrics.description: If the meaning or effect of the story depends on a particular background or peculiar civilization, the method should allow that background to be clearly seen, often requiring pictorial exposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Nanda’s world in The Awkward Age is a singular tract; if the environment’s quality is crucial to meaning, drama alone may not suffice; the novelist may justifiably supply pictorial material to ground the action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid gratuitous authorial commentary ('spokesman' anti-pattern)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not let an omniscient authorial voice intrude to explain or moralize where the action could reveal the issue; excessive commentary often 'embarrasses' the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The critic objects to the showman narrator who 'talks and talks about an issue that might be revealing itself without him.' Use commentary only when it contributes necessary perspective or economy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Difficulty/trade-off: strict drama is hard to sustain
rubrics_metrics.description: Treating a subject with the full rigour of pure drama is extremely difficult; many novelists rely on omniscience because it is easier to explain minds than to make action alone enact them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be mindful of authorial skill and ambition: choose strict drama only if the subject and the writer's capacity justify it; otherwise mixed methods may better serve the work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pictorial preparation as propulsion (Balzac's method)
rubrics_metrics.description: Massing pictorial detail and creating a vivid setting in advance can provide propulsive force for subsequent action; setting can supply character and energy to the drama.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balzac is praised for carefully creating scenes (e.g., Maison Vauquer) and hoarding life until it will 'carry the story forward with a strong sweep.' But be wary of indulging in irrelevant minutiae.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious reusing characters across works (avoid irrelevant associations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reintroducing characters with rich pasts from other books may add a sense of unity to a cycle, but in a single story their irrelevant histories can distract and obstruct the foreground action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a background character's past is unrelated to the current protagonist's world, that extra association 'detracts' from the immediacy of the present story. Use overlapping characters only when their histories serve the current narrative purpose.
